articles.title: ‘Triangle of Sadness’ Producer Backs Park Syeyoung’s Memory-Bending Love Motel Drama ‘Satellite of Love’ at Busan Asian Project Market
articles.summary: A woman who has spent a decade shut inside a room at a rural love motel, waiting for the man who left her, discovers that the motel has been staging her love life all along in “Satellite of Love,” the fourth feature from South Korean filmmaker Park Syeyoung (“The Fin”). The project is part of
body: A decade on, a man turns up saying he is the one who left. She doesn’t know his face, but he keeps at it, and slowly they fall in love. Then the cracks show. Their conversations start to loop. When he pleads with her to run away with him, the motel’s managers take him away.

The truth is that the motel exists to keep the woman’s feelings alive and replay them. Men brought in from outside are coached to act out romances with her again and again, performing love, regret and guilt while their tears are gathered. Once she knows this, she goes back to her routine and turns her eyes to the door, waiting again for someone to come back.

“I hope to convey the way in which our memories are so volatile and how the present can keep altering what has happened in the past,” Park says. “How nothing is definite and every memory is subject to change.”

Paramount Primal’s upcoming slate includes “Boys for Life,” with Alex Wolff, set for theatrical release on April 9, 2027; “Sweet Spot,” a high-concept thriller spec from writing duo Nic Curcio and Kirby Gladstein; and “The Troop,” based on the acclaimed horror novel by Nick Cutter. The label also recently acquired the U.S. rights to adapt the original screenplay for “A Nightmare on Elm Street” from the Wes Craven estate, and is developing the R-rated fantasy “Tower Defense” from writer Evan Daugherty.

articles.title: ‘Below’ Creator Breaks Down the Finale’s Last Shot, Josh Hartnett’s Accent and Season 2 Clues
articles.summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the first season of “Below,” now streaming on Netflix. Netflix’s new mystery series “Below” has arrived, and audiences are being transported to the beautiful and dangerous Newfoundland town of Snook’s Arm.
body: Variety spoke with “Below” creator and showrunner Jesse McKeown and executive producer Jessica Rhoades about Season 1’s ending, how the cast tackled the Newfoundland accent, the giant squid’s development and what might be explored in a second season.

Jesse McKeown: I’ve been going to Newfoundland for many, many years, and I had just always had a dream of making something there — something that was really big. There are a lot of smaller things that have been made in Newfoundland. There’s a strong film and television community there, but it’s very small. I wanted to do something that took advantage of the drama of the place. I never thought that would happen, but then, in a meeting with Netflix, an opportunity opened up and I snagged it and pitched them this and they went for it.

Jessica Rhoades: I mean, you had to. I’d like to say it was some brilliant, bold move, but you have to get it right. Jesse has family in Newfoundland. He wasn’t going to be allowed to go home if we got it wrong. So the stakes are high. But both Josh — and Charlie [Heaton], and a few of the other actors like Ruby [Stokes] out of the U.K. — had done accent work. So they dove in.

articles.title: ‘Other Mommy’: Five Biggest Changes From the Book, Including a Crazy Death Scene and a Much Darker Ending
articles.summary: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers from “Other Mommy,” now playing in theaters. “Other Mommy” is battling less-than-enthusiastic reviews in order to lead the weekend box office, thanks to a viral trailer that scared audiences nationwide.
body: Below, Variety has gathered the five biggest differences between the book and the film, from one jaw-dropping scene the movie adds to the much darker ending of the book.

In “Other Mommy,” the demon is skilled at mimicking humans during the whole runtime. There are moments where, as Other Mommy, it has specific tells, like face drooping or levitation slightly off the floor. But largely it’s a convincing mimic.

There are more signs of something nefarious in the book, as the demon is more avian in appearance, has less steady facial features, carries a putrid smell and an essence that causes some people to cough.

One of the key scenes of the film is a séance set up by Grandma Ruth (Karen Allen), which ends with a well-equipped but naive ghost hunting squad conjuring Other Mommy, and getting unceremoniously killed for their troubles.

Does it really matter which film is the highest-grossing of all time at the global box office?
body: And yet the most interesting thing about Avengers: Endgame’s return to cinemas is not how much money it has made – for the record, the rerelease, titled Avengers Endgame: Encore, had brought in another $126m worldwide by last weekend, taking its lifetime total to approximately $2.925bn (just ahead of Avatar’s $2.923bn) – but what Marvel added to the picture while we were all busy counting.

Premium-format presentations of the new version feature a new scene at the end of the film and another three during and after its credits, with some also appearing in standard screenings. The idea is presumably that these tantalising snippets will segue viewers smoothly into the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday with the sort of spring in the step that can only come from being convinced that they are now three tiny clues away from understanding the mind of Kevin Feige.

body: Tenzing, a former Sherpa guide whose unparalleled knowledge of the mountain and exemplary climbing skills earned him promotion to full team member, is played here by Tibetan actor Genden Phuntsok, while Hillary is robustly portrayed by Tom Hiddleston. Screenwriter Luke Davies and director Jennifer Peedom have the decent aim of restoring Tenzing’s achievement to the centre of the narrative, a tale which at the time was resoundingly claimed for Hillary and the British empire: a glorious redemption of Scott’s Antarctic ordeal 41 years earlier and a sign of divine approval for the imminent coronation of Queen Elizabeth II.

articles.title: Lost generation: the AI threat to Britain’s next great directors
articles.summary: Commercials once launched careers from Ridley Scott to Guy Ritchie, now automated production is cutting costs – and the chance to learn by doing. When Ridley Scott was awarded the UK’s highest accolade for a glittering career directing films from Alien and Blade Runner to Gladiator and The Martian…
body: The advertising industry has long been a breeding ground for British film and TV talent who have gone on to make the jump to Hollywood productions, including Guy Ritchie, who started out making music videos and commercials, and Paddington in Peru director Dougal Wilson, whose credits include a number of John Lewis’s famous Christmas ads.

But the panicked race to introduce AI technology across the advertising industry, to cut client costs and avoid being pushed aside by big tech, has raised fears of a lost generation who may be denied the opportunity to develop into great British film and TV directors.
“100%, yes, I have fears,” says Luke Scott, who runs the group that includes Ridley Scott Associates, the media production company that was co-founded by his father in the 1960s.

“I’m grown up enough to recognise that change is inevitable. But what I’ve seen generally in terms of generative AI output is a very mixed bag. You can turn to it and do something and say ‘Look what I made and isn’t it edifying’. But that is very misleading and sort of introducing us to an ersatz creativity.

articles.title: Lightsaber Darth Vader used in ‘I am your father’ Star Wars duel up for auction
articles.summary: Saber is expected to fetch at least $1m and is one of more than two dozen props that will be up for sale. A lightsaber used by Darth Vader in the Star Wars duel where he tells Luke Skywalker “I am your father” is going up for sale at Heritage Auctions next month.
body: The Vader saber, also used in Return of the Jedi, is expected to fetch at least $1m. It is one of more than two dozen lightsaber props that will be up for sale at the auction that spans Star Wars Episodes I through IX and other films and TV shows from the universe George Lucas created.
Others include dueling lightsabers wielded by Ewan McGregor’s Obi-Wan Kenobi and Hayden Christensen’s Anakin Skywalker in Revenge of the Sith that are expected to go for at least $10,000 apiece.

In July, a lightsaber with Luke Skywalker’s severed hand from The Empire Strikes Back sold for $3.75m at auction, the highest price ever fetched for a prop used in a Star Wars film according to the auction house.
An EE-3 carbine blaster wielded by Boba Fett throughout The Empire Strikes Back is estimated to bring in more than $100,000.

articles.title: Hollywood actor Luke Evans on 'joyous' four months filming in rainy Wales
articles.summary: His family were on the set, and he even managed to get some relatives a cameo in the final episode.
body: Hollywood actor Luke Evans said filming just 25 minutes from his childhood home was "joyous" - and some family members even made a cameo in the final episode of his new drama.
The Pontypool-born star, who is also an executive producer of the five-part series, The Party, came up with the idea to adapt the acclaimed novel by Elizabeth Day into a drama for the screen.
For the first time in 30 years, Evans was able to film close to Aberbargoed, Caerphilly county, where he grew up, as the drama was shot in Cardiff and Bridgend.
The star of Beauty and the Beast, Immortals and The Hobbit had been used to being far from home while working on the stage and films.

articles.title: Iliza Shlesinger and Mira Sorvino to Receive Top Honors at San Diego International Film Festival
articles.summary: The pair, set to receive Virtuoso and Trailblazer awards, will be feted at the Night of the Stars tribute at La Jolla's Conrad Prebys Performing Arts Center on Oct. 13.
body: Iliza Shlesinger and Mira Sorvino will take a spin in the spotlight at the Night of the Stars tribute as they receive top honors from the San Diego International Film Festival.

Shlesigner meanwhile will receive a Trailblazer honor as a “visionary whose groundbreaking work has challenged convention, opened doors and helped shape the future of the entertainment industry.” The stand-up star, whose next special Iliza Shlesigner: A Different Animal bows on Prime Video next March, segued to the big screen with a romantic comedy titled Chasing Summer. After debuting at Sundance, the Josephine Decker-directed pic has also been selected to screen at SDIFF.

“Both Mira Sorvino and Iliza Shlesinger represent the extraordinary range of talent and artistry that we celebrate at the San Diego International Film Festival,” said Tonya Mantooth, SDIFF CEO and artistic director. “Mira’s remarkable performances have demonstrated a depth, intelligence, and versatility that continue to resonate with audiences, while Iliza has forged a distinctive voice that has expanded the possibilities of comedy and storytelling.”
